items.title: Quantum algorithms for multidimensional partial differential equations
items.subtitle: Quantum linear-algebra methods for scientific PDE workloads
items.summary: Research on quantum and hybrid quantum-classical methods for solving multidimensional PDEs, including circuit-efficient formulations, practical case studies, and singular-value-based approaches for scientific workloads.
overview: This research explores how quantum linear-algebra techniques can be used to formulate and solve multidimensional partial differential equations that arise across scientific and engineering applications.
The work emphasizes practical circuit structure, scalability, and validation across representative PDE families rather than treating the quantum algorithm as an isolated mathematical primitive.

sections.heading: Research direction
paragraphs: The central question is how to map structured PDE problems into quantum computations while keeping the circuit construction efficient enough to study on simulators and available hardware.

Recent work extends this direction toward quantum singular-value decomposition and transformation and hybrid quantum-classical workflows for computational fluid dynamics and nuclear-physics equations.

items.title: Particle Track Reconstruction
items.subtitle: End-to-end C++ track reconstruction with helical state estimation, global hit ownership, trajectory completion, and deterministic fragment closure
items.summary: A clean-room C++ particle-track reconstruction system focused on reconstruction closure: helical state estimation, hit ownership, trajectory completion, and fragment suppression. Measured ablations on the current revision show that completion/closure is the decisive quality step: disabling it leaves 693 tracks for 500 references with a 27.27% duplicate rate, while the full pipeline returns exactly 500 tracks with 0% fake and duplicate rates.
items.visualAlt: Transverse detector view showing hundreds of measured TrackML particle trajectories radiating from the collision region.
items.visualCaption: Transverse view of the controlled 500-track TrackML validation subset from event000001000, generated from measured hit coordinates.
overview: Particle Track Reconstruction is a native C++ research platform for studying how detector hits become a final, globally consistent set of trajectories. Six interchangeable branch/search policies feed the same downstream reconstruction core, which handles fitting, hit ownership, trajectory completion, and fragment closure.

The measured evidence separates the contributions. Search policy changes compute cost more than final quality on the controlled subset; trajectory completion and fragment closure eliminate a large duplicate-track failure mode; and shared-hit collaboration is workload-dependent rather than automatically beneficial.

sections.heading: Reconstruction focus
paragraphs: The branch policy is intentionally interchangeable. EKF, A*, ant colony, particle swarm, simulated annealing, and Hungarian-style search all feed the same downstream reconstruction path for helical state estimation, hit ownership, trajectory completion, fragment suppression, and final collection building.
The measured ablations below separate search policy from the reconstruction machinery, which makes the downstream contribution visible without relying on a schematic illustration.

sections.heading: Closure ablation
paragraphs: The strongest measured effect is downstream of branch generation. With the full reconstruction stack, the controlled 500-track subset closes to exactly 500 reconstructed tracks with 100% efficiency, 0% fake rate, and 0% duplicate rate.

Disabling trajectory completion and its fragment-closure path keeps efficiency at 100%, but the output expands to 693 tracks: 27.27% duplicates and 0.58% fakes. Disabling refinement alone does not change the final 500-track result. This isolates completion/closure as the step that removes the dominant redundant-fragment failure mode on this workload.

figures.alt: Measured closure ablation. Full reconstruction has zero fake and duplicate rates. Without trajectory completion and closure, duplicate rate is 27.27 percent and fake rate is 0.58 percent while efficiency remains 100 percent.
figures.caption: Measured ablation at revision 48a913c. Rates are computed from the same controlled 500-track TrackML subset.

sections.heading: Branch-policy comparison
paragraphs: Five of the six branch policies—EKF, A*, ACO, PSO, and simulated annealing—produce the same perfect final quality on the controlled subset: 100% efficiency, 0% fake rate, 0% duplicate rate, and exactly 500 reconstructed tracks. Hungarian-style assignment also reaches 100% efficiency and 0% fake rate, but leaves one duplicate track.

The policies differ more clearly in compute cost. On one thread, EKF, ACO, PSO, and SA cluster near 3.8 ms per event, A* is about 4.0 ms, and Hungarian is about 7.6 ms in the measured three-repetition median.

figures.alt: Horizontal bar chart of median single-thread reconstruction time: EKF 3.78 milliseconds, A star 4.00, ACO 3.79, PSO 3.80, simulated annealing 3.82, and Hungarian 7.62.
figures.caption: Measured branch-policy compute comparison. Same event subset, same reconstruction core, one thread, three-repetition medians.

figures.alt: Duplicate-rate comparison across branch policies. EKF, A star, ACO, PSO, and simulated annealing are at zero percent; Hungarian is at 0.20 percent. All six have 100 percent efficiency and zero fake rate.
figures.caption: Final-track quality by branch policy. The downstream closure stack makes final quality largely insensitive to the search policy on this controlled subset.

sections.heading: Thread scaling
paragraphs: The EKF reconstruction path scales from 115.6k reconstructed tracks/s at one thread to 185.4k tracks/s at eight threads on the controlled subset, a 1.60× throughput increase while preserving the same 100% efficiency and zero fake/duplicate result.

This event is small enough that sixteen threads are counterproductive: median throughput falls to 39.8k tracks/s. The scaling curve therefore shows the practical saturation point rather than implying linear speedup.

figures.alt: TrackReco thread-scaling plot showing 115.6 thousand tracks per second at one thread, 150.3 thousand at two, 173.9 thousand at four, 185.4 thousand at eight, and 39.8 thousand at sixteen.
figures.caption: Measured TrackReco thread scaling on the controlled 500-track subset. Median of nine repetitions per thread count.

sections.heading: Same-machine mkFit timing reference
paragraphs: A fresh mkFit devel build was run on the same Jupiter CPU using the same 500-track TrackML selection converted through the TrackML adapter. At one thread, TrackReco's full reconstruction-engine median is 4.33 ms, while mkFit reports 4.54 ms for its total event loop and 2.19 ms for its CloneEngine build stage. At eight threads, the corresponding medians are 2.70 ms, 2.30 ms, and 0.50 ms.

The timing scopes are not identical, so the figure is a same-machine implementation reference rather than a claim that the internal stages are equivalent. It does show that TrackReco is in the same millisecond-scale regime while performing its downstream completion and fragment-closure work.

figures.alt: Grouped timing bars comparing TrackReco reconstruction-engine latency with mkFit total event-loop latency and mkFit CloneEngine build-stage latency at one and eight threads.
figures.caption: Fresh same-machine timing reference. TrackReco revision 48a913c; mkFit devel revision ba370252. Same controlled 500-track selection, nine measured repetitions after warm-up.

sections.heading: Collaboration policy
paragraphs: Shared-hit collaboration is not automatically better. At eight threads on the controlled 500-track subset, forcing hit sharing leaves final reconstruction quality unchanged for every branch but usually reduces throughput. The measured throughput change versus sharing disabled ranges from +0.6% for A* to -11.0% for ACO.

The objective-adaptive collaboration policy selects its no-sharing fallback for all six branchers on this sparse workload, avoiding collaboration when the conflict signal does not justify it. A denser 1,000-track stress subset from the same event gives the same qualitative result for EKF: off and forced-on both reconstruct 82.9% of references with identical fake/duplicate rates, while forced sharing reduces throughput by 13.1%; the adaptive policy again falls back to no sharing. The useful contribution is therefore workload-aware collaboration, not an always-on claim.

figures.alt: Measured collaboration ablation showing throughput change when hit sharing is forced on versus off: EKF minus 6.8 percent, A star plus 0.6 percent, ACO minus 11.0 percent, PSO minus 1.5 percent, simulated annealing minus 10.4 percent, and Hungarian minus 9.5 percent. Final reconstruction quality is unchanged.
figures.caption: Measured collaboration ablation, eight threads and five-repetition medians. Adaptive collaboration disables sharing on this workload rather than paying the fixed-sharing overhead.

sections.heading: Current validation
paragraphs: The published configuration is validated on a fixed public TrackML subset built from event000001000: the 500 highest-pT charged particles with pT at least 0.5 GeV, |eta| at most 2.5, and at least four recorded hits. The selected workload contains 5,605 measured hits.

Starting from the measured hits, the automatic reconstruction pipeline returns exactly 500 tracks for the 500 reference trajectories, with zero fake tracks and zero duplicate tracks. Four disjoint 250-track robustness windows from the same public event also reach 100% reconstruction efficiency; across those windows, fake rate spans 0.38–1.16% and duplicate rate spans 1.94–3.46%. These are scoped validation results, not a claim of perfect reconstruction for arbitrary detectors or occupancies.

sections.heading: Research questions
items: How should local track-state estimation and global hit assignment be coupled?
How should incomplete trajectories be extended without pulling in hits from nearby particles?
How can overlapping and non-overlapping fragments be recognized as one trajectory without merging distinct tracks?
When does collaborative hit sharing improve reconstruction enough to justify its synchronization cost?
Which search policies give the best reconstruction quality-compute tradeoff under bounded candidate growth?

sections.heading: Validation scope
paragraphs: The 100% figure is end-to-end automatic reconstruction efficiency on the fixed 500-track validation subset. It describes the final track collection after fitting, conflict resolution, trajectory completion, and fragment closure.

The branch, collaboration, closure, thread-scaling, and mkFit timing figures are fresh measurements from the current TrackReco revision. The robustness windows and 1,000-track stress subset come from the same TrackML event, so they broaden within-event evidence but do not establish multi-event or experiment-wide performance.
